description:
Although I don't normally make Vanilla Ice Cream, I thought it was about time I gave you this amazing homemade vanilla ice cream recipe. 

This video gives you just a brief history of Vanilla ice cream and we also make 2 types, a French Vanilla Custard ice cream and Philly style Vanilla ice cream. 

I much prefer the custard version, it's rich and full of body and flavour and I highly recommend you try making it. 

If you enjoyed this video, please consider liking and subscribing, plus pop over to our Instagram and Facebook pages linked below and say hello :)

Instagram: https://tinyurl.com/2p85zcxh
Facebook: http://tiny.cc/mmxosz
Website: https://www.polaricecreamery.com


Thanks and see you on the next video :)

#vanilla #vanillaicecream #icecream #icecreamrecipe #gelato #vanillabeans

comments.text: Hi Nick. I noticed that a couple of your recipes call for the cream to be added after the cooking process, in essence adding the chilled cream just before churning. Salt & Straw also do this. However, most of your recipes combine the milk and cream together on the cooktop. Is there a 'better' time to be adding the cream to the various ice cream recipes? Thanks
comments.author: @febsat

comments.text: Honestly, it depends on the quality of the cream. The cream here in 🇨🇦 is pretty poor so by cooking it out, it removes and fatty mouthfeel. UK cream was so good, it didn’t really need to be cooked out. Sometimes the recipe just all needs to be cooked though because if ingredients etc.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: @PolarIceCreamery  Thank you. I may try a few of the recipes both ways to see if there is a noticeable difference. Cheers.
comments.author: @febsat

comments.text:
Nick,

Growing up in the United States in the state of Louisiana a childhood friend’s mother made peach ice cream using a vanilla base.  She passed away thirty years ago…. & I have tried & tried to duplicate her recipe, but never doing so. I have tried for 25 years…. at least.  

Last night I tried again, but this time having had the advantage of spending hour after hour learning from you.  

This morning I opened the freezer & tasted last night’s batch.   I wish I could give you a scoop!   We did it!   I have 100% duplicated the ice cream of my childhood!

A million “Thanks!”

Ben
comments.author: @benboyd-xo1qp

comments.text: Nice!! I’m glad you finally managed to make your Louisiana Peach ice cream. I’d like to make it on the channel if you wouldn’t mind sharing your process?
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text:
Nick......... I informed my family you might make a video demonstrating my vanilla base for peach ice cream & they said I am nearly famous now !  I will provide the recipe for the peach ice cream base I have worked for so many years to accomplish.  I really could not have achieved the base I remember from my childhood without your help!  

However, I have not taken the next step which will be to include peaches.  I don't know if you would recommend I try using frozen peaches.  I would give them a try if you think frozen peaches might work.  For now............. the base you helped me achieve is:    

650 G Whole Milk
800 G. Heavy Cream
380 Condensed Milk
140 G nonfat powder milk
65 G corn syrup
4 egg yolks
105 G sugar
2 t vanilla extract
2 G stabilizers (SpecialIngredients Ice Cream Stabiliser) 
1.5 G salt

This makes 2060 Grams

Thank you for helping me reach back to my childhood in Louisiana & achieve something I have tried for so many years to create!      @PolarIceCreamery
comments.author: @benboyd-xo1qp

comments.text:
Hey nick, what role does msnf play in ice cream? How do you decide how much of it? The calculator has a recommendation but seems a bit arbitrary. 

Along with that, what relative sweetness do you aim for? And PAT?
comments.author: @mohamedsharif9736

comments.text:
MSNF is the protein, minerals and lactose required for good overrun, structure and viscosity of the ice cream. I usually try for 10% but if adding alcohol, increase to 12%. 
Relative sweetness is a big subject and depends a lot on the ice cream being made. I will go in to this in the sugars video.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery
